text: Hokas and On Clouds are the worst shoes you can pack for New York City. I know that'll upset people, but it is not the brand. It is the design.

If you just spent nearly two hundred dollars on Hokas or On Clouds specifically for your New York trip, do not put them in your suitcase. Those plush gym shoes are built for forty minutes on a treadmill, not 20,000 steps on unforgiving city concrete.

Watch what happens to anyone wearing Hokas or On Clouds around two in the afternoon in New York. They'll be either icing their heels in the hotel or paying 40 dollars for a cab because their feet completely tapped out before dinner.

These shoes are built to move a runner forward for forty minutes, not for someone exploring New York City. When you are visiting Manhattan, you are not just walking. You are pounding solid concrete, climbing three flights of subway stairs, navigating cracked pavement, standing in lines for hours, and doing it all for eight, nine, sometimes ten hours straight. Three things people overlook until they are already in the city.

Number one, that soft foam feeling and those bouncy pods do not tell you the whole story. With Hokas, that thick soft foam is made to spring a runner forward on a jog. But New York means walking six blocks, standing in line for a bagel, waiting on a concrete subway platform, and standing through a museum tour because the line does not get shorter when your feet start aching from the foam packing flat. And with On Clouds, those hollow open pods compress down under constant concrete standing, leaving your arch with zero support right when you need it most.

Number two, Hokas and On Clouds were not built for city streets and winter hazards. In New York, you are walking across cracked pavement, stepping off icy curbs, and hurrying down steep subway stairs for hours. You want to feel steady with every step. With Hokas, that massive, tall stack height shifts your balance, making you wobble over frozen slush and putting extra strain directly on your knees and ankles. Plus, all that thick foam makes them heavy to lift over twenty thousand steps. And with On Clouds, those smooth pod outsoles turn into literal ice skates the second winter slush, snow, or freezing rain hits polished station tile and metal subway grates. That is where a slip-resistant outsole matters. You want a shoe with real grip, not an unstable sole or slippery pods on freezing streets.

Number three, the toe box is narrow, and it does not stretch. On Clouds are notoriously narrow to lock a runner tight, and Hokas taper sharply at the toes. If they squeeze your toes together before you have even left the hotel, that is not a promising start. After hours of walking eight to ten miles across the city, your feet naturally swell. A tight fit becomes the only thing you can think about. Your toes feel trapped, rubbing blisters with every single block. You are loosening your laces on a bench in Central Park, and you have still got dinner and a Broadway show to go.

That is why Comfortwear built the opposite of a running shoe, made for people whose feet have to get through real life: nurses, healthcare workers, and travelers who want to actually enjoy the trip they have been saving for. A roomy toe box lets your toes spread out instead of getting squeezed together. A flexible stretch knit upper gives your feet room as they swell throughout the day. Comfortable cushioning and built-in arch support work together underfoot so the support never packs flat, paired with a slip-resistant outsole for added traction on wet crosswalks, subway stairs, and metal grates.

Because you do not want to be the person cutting the day short, sitting on a bench in Soho watching everyone else explore, or tapping out and paying fifty dollars for an Uber back to the hotel. You want to be walking the Brooklyn Bridge, exploring every neighborhood, and there when the curtain goes up at the theater.
